explanation: Quadratic functions can be written in [[kw:intercept form]]: $ f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q) $, where $ a \ne 0 $.
The [[kw:x-intercepts]] (also called [[kw:zeros]]) are $ p $ and $ q $. These are the points where the graph crosses the x-axis.
The [[kw:axis of symmetry]] is halfway between the x-intercepts: $$ x = \frac{p + q}{2} $$
The [[kw:vertex]] lies on the axis of symmetry. Find its x-coordinate using the formula, then plug into the function to get the y-coordinate.
If $ a > 0 $, the parabola opens upward; if $ a < 0 $, it opens downward.

formulaCard.title: Intercept Form of a Quadratic Function

discoveryHook.scenario: If a quadratic is written as a product of factors like (x−p)(x−q), the x-intercepts jump right out: they're p and q! No graphing needed. The axis of symmetry runs right down the middle, and the vertex sits on that axis. It's the quickest way to sketch a parabola!

confusionCorner.title: Signs in the Factors
confusionCorner.body: The intercept form uses $(x - p)$. If a factor is $(x + 4)$, then $p = -4$. [[imp:The x-intercept is the opposite of the number you see.]] For $(x - 3)$, the intercept is $3$; for $(x + 1)$, it's $-1$.

formulaCard.title: From Standard to Intercept Form

explanation: Many standard form quadratics $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ can be factored into intercept form $f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q)$.
To rewrite: 1) Factor out the GCF if there is one. 2) Factor the remaining trinomial or use special patterns (difference of squares, perfect square trinomial).
Once in intercept form, the x-intercepts are $p$ and $q$, and you can find the axis of symmetry and vertex as before.

teacherCues: Write $f(x)=2x^2-8$. 'Factor out the GCF: $2(x^2-4)$. Then difference of squares: $2(x+2)(x-2)$.'
Now we can read the intercepts: $-2$ and $2$. Graph from there.

confusionCorner.body: If there's a common factor, factor it out before looking for binomial factors. In $4x^2 - 36x + 32$, factor out 4: $4(x^2 - 9x + 8) = 4(x-1)(x-8)$. The intercepts are 1 and 8, not divided by 4.
confusionCorner.title: GCF First!

blocks.title: Finding Zeros Using Intercept Form

confusionCorner.body: If a factor is squared, like $(x-2)^2$, the zero $x=2$ is a repeated root. It's still a valid zero, and the graph touches the x-axis there without crossing.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Repeated Zero

questions.prompt: The Zero-Product Property says if $(x-p)(x-q)=0$, then $x-p=0$ or $x-q=0$, so the zeros are $p$ and ___.
hints: The two numbers in the intercept form.

questions.prompt: Find the zeros of $g(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 12$. (Type the single zero)
How many zeros does $h(x) = x(x^2-1)$ have?

explanation: A [[kw:zero]] of a function is an x-value where $f(x) = 0$. It's the same as an x-intercept.
For any function in intercept form $f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q) ...$, set the function equal to 0 and apply the [[kw:Zero-Product Property]].
If the function is not in intercept form, factor it first. Look for GCF, trinomial patterns, difference of squares.
This works for cubics too: $h(x) = (x-1)(x^2-16) = (x-1)(x+4)(x-4)$ → zeros at $-4, 1, 4$.

formulaCard.formula: $$ f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{zeros: } x = p, q $$
formulaCard.title: Zeros from Intercept Form
notes: For cubic: $f(x) = a(x-p)(x-q)(x-r)$ → zeros at $p, q, r$.

explanation: To graph a quadratic using its zeros: 1) Write the function in intercept form by factoring. 2) Identify and plot the x-intercepts (zeros). 3) Find and draw the axis of symmetry $x = \frac{p+q}{2}$. 4) Find and plot the vertex. 5) Use the y-intercept (from standard form or $f(0)$) as an additional point if needed. 6) Draw the parabola.
This method works because the intercept form gives the x-intercepts instantly, and symmetry gives the vertex.
For quadratics with only one zero (repeated), the vertex is on the x-axis, and that zero is the only x-intercept.

discoveryHook.scenario: With intercept form, you can build a quadratic or cubic function from just its x-intercepts and one additional point! It's like being handed the skeleton of a graph and filling in the exact curve.

formulaCard.title: Building Functions from Zeros
formulaCard.formula: $$ f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q) \quad\text{or}\quad f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q)(x - r) $$

explanation: Understand: Given x-intercepts (and possibly other conditions), choose the appropriate form: quadratic → $f(x) = a(x-p)(x-q)$; cubic → $f(x) = a(x-p)(x-q)(x-r)$.
Solve: Substitute the intercepts for $p, q$ (and $r$). Use an additional point $(x_1, y_1)$ to solve for $a$.
Conclude: Write the function in intercept form, then expand to standard form if required. The value of $a$ determines the stretch and direction.
This blueprint works for both quadratics and cubics.
